caption:
Same $150,000 profit. $9,250 less tax. Here's the difference (sole traders, 2026–27).

Owner A does nothing: income tax plus Medicare levy on $150,000, less the $1,000 small business offset = $38,570.

Owner B makes two moves before 30 June:
- Puts $20,000 into their own super and claims the deduction.
- Buys a $15,000 machine the business needed and uses the instant asset write-off.

Taxable income drops to $115,000. Personal tax and Medicare, less the offset: $26,320. Add 15% contributions tax on the $20,000 inside the fund: $3,000. Total $29,320.

The gap: $9,250.

The catch: B spent $35,000 to get it. The super is locked until retirement and the machine is only a win if the business needed it. It suits an owner who wanted both anyway, and it's the kind of plan a registered adviser should check against your numbers.

Which owner are you this year?

Narrated by an AI voice.

#smallbusinessaustralia #taxplanning #keepmore #soletrader #superannuation
figures_checked: Resident rates 2026–27: nil to $18,200; 15c to $45,000; $4,020 + 30c to $135,000; $31,020 + 37c to $190,000; $51,370 + 45c above; Medicare levy 2% not included (ATO Tax rates – Australian residents, checked 15 Nov 2026)

Small business income tax offset: 16% of tax on net small business income, capped at $1,000, aggregated turnover under $5 million, sole traders and partners only, 2026–27 (ATO Small business income tax offset, checked 15 Nov 2026)
Concessional contributions cap $32,500 for 2026–27 (ATO Key super rates and thresholds, checked 15 Nov 2026)

Instant asset write-off: assets costing less than $20,000 each, permanent from 1 July 2026, aggregated turnover under $10 million, first used or installed ready for use in the year (ATO Small business newsroom, updated 4 Sept 2026, checked 15 Nov 2026)
Salary-sacrificed super taxed at 15% in the fund; Division 293 above $250,000 (ATO Salary sacrificing super, checked 11 Nov 2026; Div 293 threshold re-confirmed 15 Nov 2026)
